You (with zero coding experience) can now create websites from scratch using AI in less than 20 minutes with this template:

In this video @anshnanda and I walk you through the process of:

The best part is... Next week we will show you how to create API endpoints, and you'll be able to create full web apps with multiple AI features.

- it'll prompt about passphrase again, just press enter
- this automatically copies the ssh key to clipboard

Go to Replit
- plus sign (new tab) and type SSH
- go to SSH panel
- Click Keys
- Add SSH Key
- Give it Label (doesn't matter what you call it)

- Copy the Shell command

- Click Add new SSH Host
- Paste the command again
- Enter
- Click the first option that pops up
- Bottom Right of screen click connect
- Click Continue
- Open Folder
- Click name of Replit Project (Repl)

title: Build an AI Army With Claude Code’s New Sub-Agents

text:
Claude Code just released sub-agents.

IN THIS VIDEO:

1. I'm giving a breakdown of what Claude Code's new Subagents feature is

2. Creating a master agent that delegates tasks to specialized subagents

3. Demo how these agents can operate in parallel

4. See how they handle different tools, including API integrations with X and FAL for social media postings and image generation

ClaudeCode has subagents for the web but if you want to build your own version of this on your phone, you should definitely check out VibeCode: https://vibecode.go.link/1kMAR

title: How I’m Actually Using Claude Duet (After 10 Hours of Testing)

text:
Every added layer of complexity in an application makes it 10x harder to describe and make content on. 

Back in April I was making many videos on Codex. 

"Codex, OpenAI's version of Claude Code" 
"Codex, the desktop app on your computer"
"Codex, the super app that can do any CPU task"

Very, very easy to describe. 
Repeatable, and viral. 

This made it effortless to describe on short form or long from videos.

Then ChatGPT and Codex merged. 

Okay, now Codex is not an app. 
Codex is a feature inside ChatGPT. 

"Codex, the AI coding agent feature inside the ChatGPT Desktop app"

Okay, now ChatGPT has "GPT Work"

"Codex, the AI coding agent feature inside the ChatGPT desktop app that allows you to do coding tasks, and sometimes work tasks, some of those should be done inside GPT Work, which is kind of similar, but like different, depending on if you are using Cloud GPT Work, or local GPT work, in which case is alot closer to Codex, but still not quite the same. If you try and use the skills you created on Codex they won't work when doing a cloud GPT Work session but if it's a local session it will work."

We haven't even made it to Codex Cloud sessions, GPT Dots, and GPT Plugins yet. 

This goes for anyone building software. If you want to create an ecosystem of creators who talk about your product organically, you should aim for simplicity.

BTW not saying it was the wrong decision for OpenAI to merge them, i'm just saying for me it got much harder to describe with every new feature added.

My unfiltered thoughts on personal agents.

Grokbot has the best UI and it’s arguably the best overall. In a lot of ways they’re ahead. Their desktop app feels the best, and their multi-bot coordination is great: you can set a team lead and it passes tasks to the other bots. Grokbot also has the best “webhook” feature, which means you can easily turn outside events into triggers that start your agents. That speeds up background workflows like watching your email, Slack and more. It also has Cursor integration, so for bigger tasks Grokbot can spin up a Cursor cloud session with any model (until OpenAI cuts SpaceX off from their models, which I think will happen soon). Unfortunately, running frontier models through Cursor costs more than Claude or Codex. Still, they’re the only ones embracing a team of agents. It’s a really cool idea, but the more bots you have, the more time you spend managing and maintaining them. I’m starting to think one bot with different threads/channels is the right answer, which I’ll get to with Claude Duet.

dots by OpenAI is rough around the edges right now, but it’s probably the most powerful if you use Codex, which I do. dots can spin up Codex sessions in the cloud or locally on your computer. So if you have coding or video editing workflows that need your local files, this is very useful. Codex computer use is also the best in the world: your dot can spin up a local Codex session that fully controls your computer, as long as it’s on. Their real-time voice is incredible. If you have your email and work tools connected, try this: go on a walk with headphones in, ask the agent to summarize your emails, have it draft replies and read them back to you, then send them off. If I remember right, this is close to a workflow you (Tim) used to have with your VAs before AI. It’s my favorite use case for personal agents. The one downside is that you have to call your agent, and it’s an awful experience. It literally rings, and it’s annoying.

Muse by Meta is a toy. I’ve talked to a bunch of finance people I play poker with who all tried it and set up automations, and they all said it doesn’t reliably do what they want. It’s fast, and its user numbers will probably keep growing. But it’s basically free: you get a TON of usage without paying a dime. That’s NOT a trade I’m willing to make. An agent doing high-leverage tasks should be running at the Opus 5.5 or GPT 6.1 Sol level.

Claude Duet - is in early access, so unfortunately not everyone can use it yet. First things first, it runs on Opus 5.5, the best model in the world. I’ve only had access for 72 hours, but Duet feels different from the others. It’s not a personified agent like Grokbot, dot or Muse, which gives it a more professional vibe that I like. When you ask your Duet agent to do something, it spins up a task, which is a new chat thread. All your threads show up in a Tasks tab, so it’s easy to see everything Duet is working on or has finished. And instead of creating more agents (like Grokbot), you create channels, just like Slack (I can tell @anthropic is Slack-pilled). I have a content channel, a finances channel, etc., which keeps different kinds of tasks separate. The only other app I’ve seen do this is Buzz by @jack, and it’s a good experience. Their strong point is documents (artifacts). If you want decks, high-quality docs or design mockups, Opus just wins. Period. It’s not close right now. Their weak point is real-time voice. It’s the worst of the bunch and borderline unusable, though I think they only added it a few days ago.

Instinct lives in iMessage, has no app, and doesn’t do anything notable besides show you product suggestions you didn’t ask for. (Not ads, according to their team.)

My hot take: 
The VM is overrated. SpaceX, OpenAI and Meta all talk about the VM your agent can use and feature it in their marketing. It’s not as useful as you’d think, because more and more websites block bots that visit their site on the cloud VM. All of these companies promise their agents can make payments, but most payments either take forever or get blocked altogether. SpaceX has a cool workaround with Grokbot that routes traffic through your computer so it uses your IP address. But I’d much rather the agent just USE my computer for the task, like dot does by handing it off to Codex. Also, i don't think normal people care about the virtual computer. If anything they get offended they have to "stream a computer". 

The problem with personal agents: by the time you read this, pick one, and test it for 7 days, every one of them will have released 10 new features and the whole landscape will have changed. It’s nearly impossible to keep up.

Codex is amazing for 3D printing. 

And Bambu Studio runs in the Dots VM which makes it even more fun.

text:
The Fable of Clawd

A 2 minute 4K film made entirely in Blender, from one prompt on Fable 5.2. It took about 4.5 hours.

Claude built every asset in Blender by writing Python:
- 5 characters and props: Clawd, his friend Pip, a toy truck, a 3D-printed tulip and a gift box
- 7 full sets: a study, a staircase, a street, a workshop, an airport, a night sky and a house
- every camera move and every frame of animation across 52 shots

That came to 12,500 lines of code. It started 7 copies of itself to build the sets at the same time.

Then it rented 89 GPUs through RunPod to render 3,220 frames as fast as possible, 36 of them running at once. Total cost: a little over $20.

My biggest takeaway is my Claude Code knows it has access to cloud compute, so it's much more ambitious.

I tried a similar prompt on my other computer that doesn't have the runpod skill setup and it wasn't nearly as high quality

Full details linked below.
Here are the video details (very detailed)

The shift is already happening

Agentic video editing is already exploding. Thousands of creators have stopped editing by hand and started directing AI to edit for them. This is only the beginning. In 18 months, editing a video manually will feel totally insane, the same way writing code by hand already does.

We've seen this movie before with Programming.

Back in 2025, a small group of developers (and non devs, like me) were early adopters of a tool called Claude Code. Slowly, then all at once, developers moved out of traditional IDEs and into agent-first tools like Claude Code, Codex and others. In 2025, most people would have told you it was crazy to leave the IDE behind. Now that's the norm.

I believe Premiere Pro is the IDE for video editors / creators.

Today, Developers still open an IDE, but only when they have to. That's exactly where the Premiere Pro and Davinci Resolve timeline is headed. Most of an editors time will be spent talking to an AI chatbot, likely in Claude Code or Codex. When something goes wrong, the editor may decide to open the timeline.

The 10x editor

In software, we're already watching the rise of the 10x programmer, and even the 100x programmer: people who set up the systems (software factories) that let AI build and improve the software for them.

A new kind of person is about to walk into companies: the 10x editor, or really, the creative producer. They won't be measured by how fast they can cut. They'll be measured by how much great content they can put out without ever lowering the bar on quality or brand.

And they'll do it by building content factories, the same way developers are building software factories right now.

We're in the early innings of agentic editing

Currently, people are using AI to edit videos but people aren't setting up content factories.

When you go to Claude Code you can say something like

"Please can you look at my footage on the camera from today and make a vlog that builds our brand"

And Claude will work for 30 minutes, or maybe even 3 hours, to hand you back a real, coherent video(sometimes). It might even surprise you. My friend Muhammad Zulali made this youtube video, and Fable 5.2 edited the whole thing in a single prompt. It was genuinely good. It's on pace to get over 2M views. This was his second video ever.

But that's still rare, and it's hard to do over and over. The people who figure out how to scale great content with AI are going to make millions. Soon, tens of millions.

In order to understand how content factories will look, let's take a close look at software factories.

How it worked with Software Factories

A software factory is what happens when a developer stops writing code and starts designing the system that writes it.

For most of history, software was something a person typed out line by line, like writing a very long, very literal letter to a machine that takes everything you say at face value. Getting good at it took years. Building anything big took a team, and most of the work wasn't the idea. It was the typing, the fixing etc.

What changed is that the machine can now read plain English and do the typing itself. So the best programmers quietly stopped writing code and started building the thing that writes it: a little factory. You hand it a clear description of what you want. A handful of AI workers build different parts at the same time, other workers test what got built, and anything broken gets sent back before you ever see it. When something does go wrong, you don't simply fix the error. You write down a rule so the factory never makes that mistake again.

The software factory gets better as you use it.

When I talk to people who build software factories, I don't see craftsmen. I see directors. They have a team of agents, a token budget and software that needs building, and their job is to coordinate those resources to get it done. Anywhere they can step out of the process and let the AI work, they do. The good ones, at least.

9 months ago, software factories were not really a thing. And now they are everywhere.

That is where we are are in video editing.

How a content factory might work

Now what would this look like for content?

A factory for content is a system that produces high quality content at scale, and increases in quality over time.

The one big difference is that software is purely digital and barely has to touch the physical world, while (good) content is deeply human. People want to watch other people, so a content factory always has a human at its center: the face, the voice and the story the whole system is built around.

But other than the videos taken with real cameras the rest is just code.

Under the hood, a Premiere Pro timeline isn't really a video. It's a text file that references videos... Basically a list of instructions that says "play this clip from 0:04 to 0:09, put this title on top, lower the music here," and the software turns those instructions into something you can watch.

-
Dragging a keyframe changes one number: when the zoom starts, from 0:02 to 0:03.

-
Trimming a clip changes two timestamps: where it starts and where it ends.

-
Dropping in a cross dissolve adds one short line: a transition, half a second long.

If video editing is just code, then everything that just happened to programming is about to happen to video editing. And if editing a video becomes mostly prompting (like coding) you'll probably want AI to do most of the prompting based on a certain set of rules. Yes, this is a content factory. And we will need experts to manage these systems, while deeply understanding content, marketing, and editing.

The creative director of the future starts by understanding the whole story of the creator or company they're growing: who they are, what they believe, how they talk and what they'd never say. And they know, almost by feel, what a viewer should feel. They will still have an instinct for story and brand. They will understand the set of associations that builds up in someone's head, video after video: the pace, the music, the light, the way a story lands with different audience groups. Great creative directors shape that on purpose, so long after the video ends, the feeling stays. That part is an art form, and it's the one thing the factory can't do on its own.

Then the creative director will need to build a team, part human and part AI, that turns that story into every format at once: long-form videos, shorts, podcasts, newsletters and posts.

This is a content factory, which is as an amplifier with unlimited upside, but it can only multiply the true value at the center. If the humans at the center brings no value, it amplifies to zero... (0 x 0 = 0)

In the near term (next 3 months), not much will change. The great creators and marketers will continue to rise to the top. But I believe sometime in the next 12 months we will hit an inflection point where AI get's so good that those with content factories will takeover the entire internet.

In future newsletters I will dive deeper into actual AI workflows the best marketers use now for growing on social media while building brand.
